title: need to do a director deep-dive for a film class -- help me choose one??

commenti.body:
Hi. I’m writing a script for a movie and I want your feedback for the current title I have for the film.

The title is:

**The Radiant Anthology**

I want to know:

1. Before knowing what it’s about, what are your initial impressions of the title?

2. After knowing what it’s about, do you like it as a title for this story? Why or why not?

Here’s what it’s about:

>!A young woman journeys through a world stitched together from scenes based on classic poems she must interpret as a whole to discover a devastating truth about her life.!<

Hi there! 

So I don't know what the parameters are for your particular paper, but from an accessibility standpoint I think Haneke is the choice here based on the fact that Bunuel and Fassbinder have much larger bodies of work, and while that could result in more to chew on and more to work with, it'd also be a much more daunting research process. I also read a pretty popular post on here from a film professor who said they disliked that so many film students try to look at films from an optimistic lens. I can't name 5 more depressing/soul crushing, but incredibly rich bodies of work than Haneke's. Make your film professor happy, write about some sad shit! lol. 

Also, just personal bias here, I think Cache is one of the best films ever made. Hope that helps, and good luck on your paper!

You seem to be listing directors who are still living -- if that's your preference, I'd suggest Werner Herzog. Large body of work to choose from. Documentary & narrative. Plenty of interviews online where he discusses his philosophy. He has a Masterclass series and a newly released memoir. 

While some of his films are tricky, there are clear themes that one could blanket over his entire filmography.

You could go off the beaten path here (which should impress your professor) if you're looking at working filmmakers.  Gaspar Noe is the *enfant terrible* of contemporary auteurist cinema.  Like Haneke, he's dark, unrepentant and most certainly controversial.  His body of work is manageable in that he's made only 7 feature films.  Another one in that realm - but much more lyrical and New Wave-playful -  is Leos Carax.  He's made 6 features.

Ruben Östlund is worth a look. His work takes on a lot of big themes and does so very representationally, so it lends itself to an essay. His work to me lands fairly close to Lathimos - leaning more into satire and absurdist comedy than the truly darker side of things.

Plus he started his career shooting skiing documentaries and there is some through lines in doing long takes in his film Involuntary that could be fun discussing.

Not particularly in the same vein as Yorgos, but from an academic standpoint Robert Bresson would be a great fit for an analytical paper due to his unity of theory and practice. He wrote extensively on his films and the theory behind his approach, which is very specific and clearly conveyed in his films, all of which adhere to his meticulous philosophy. The book “Notes on the Cinematograph” is a treasure trove of short writings (notes) detailing his approach and thoughts on the specifics of the cinematic art and how it differentiates (and should, according to him) from theater. He touches on everything from directing to acting to sound to cinematography and so on. It’s kind of like Sun Tzu’s “Art of War” but for filmmakers. It is a quick read and easy read, but a must read, in my opinion. I think an analysis of his unity of theory and practice would yield very interesting conclusions not only about his work but also the very nature and essence of cinema.

I did my paper on Bob Fosse. Once you read about his life, well, analyzing his films just made sense. He invented jazz dance largely from watching strippers dance as a child. His films all include hurt, fractured women. In life he cheated on his wife a lot. So he likes women but does he? From Sweet Charity to All the Jazz, Star 80, you wonder. I liked writing about it.
